reviews.text: [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/31028489-Maddmike/]Maddmike Steam Curator[/url] Ufouria the Saga 2 is twee. It’s a fact that supersedes any conversation about its genre or its gameplay or its progression. All of those things are just vehicles to deliver a vibe—and thankfully that vibe is immaculately curated with a beautiful craft and felt aesthetic. This is a dumb little world inhabited by dumb little creatures with dumb little problems: like Mr. Jennifer and his unwillingness to join you unless you get him Pepto Bismol to alleviate his stomach issues. It effortlessly weaves non-urgent slice of life scenarios into a short but sweet metroidvania format. It’s mechanically light and beatable within an afternoon; but if you’re willing to embrace what Ufouria has on offer, that afternoon will be damn cozy. https://youtu.be/1tPcGQ1dsww You start as a singular character, Hebe, waking up in his treetop bedroom/bathroom that’s also the central hub that all the other zones sprawl out from. Not too sprawling, mind you: part of Ufouria’s short duration is owed to the fact that those zones are only ever a hop and a skip away from home-base and easily fast traveled back to when needed. It’s pretty frictionless by design: though you do have an alien with nefarious plans you have to take down, most of the game is really just doing favors for your three buddies and exploring to find secrets. The map borrows some rogue elements in its design. The world itself is consistent: Popoitto Caves is always to the east and Ufouria fields is always to the west, but once you go into one of those zones it becomes its own mini-instanced platformer level with semi-randomized layout and completion bonuses for finishing. You’ll want to get to the end and fight the boss while collecting as much currency and collectables as you can on the way, then you’re usually met with the option of proceeding to an adjacent level or porting back to home base and spending what you’ve accumulated. There’s two semi-discrete phases of the game: your first hour or two will be gathering the crew, which is a sequence of finding them out in the world, beating them in a boss fight due to some sitcom-level misunderstanding, then completing some sort of collection task for them. The second half of the game is using all of the accumulated abilities of the crew to get to all the previously inaccessible zones and collecting the prerequisites for a final boss push. Regardless of which step of the journey you’re on you’ll frequently want to take trips back to the vending machine at home which has a variety of health upgrades, utility spells, and other ways to enhance your exploration. Its randomized take on level layouts add a different texture to those metroidvania ‘come back here when you get the double jump’ moments. It’s not a specific obstacle getting in your way every time because it's random, it's usually a genre of obstacle. Getting the climb with Hebe lets you get to the high levels, getting the swim from Mr Jennifer lets you descend into the water, but outside of the non-randomized hub, it’s not like there are exact coordinates you need to remember. Just know that the swim helps you with water and make a mental note of which zones have water, rather than recall particular puddles within that zone. It’s less gratifying than your average ‘aha!’ moment that usually comes with this kind of game, but it works within the context of Efouria’s effortless difficulty. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3169903554 The combat and general movement style is simple by design, harkening back to its retro origins and also aligning to Ufouria’s felt style. Everything is just a little frumpy. Even the simple act of killing an enemy demands getting above them to butt stomp, and if you want them to sit still to enable that cleanly you’ll need to press a button to take one of your Popoons from your pocket, then another to throw it at a fixed angle at your foe. It’s not smooth, it’s not physically satisfying and, yet, it all kind of works? I couldn’t imagine your basic mode of attack being a simple strike with modern flare and tight control because that’s not what Ufouria is or what it’s going for. If that sounds like cope just remember it was like this 30 years ago, too. The first game was tone first and this one is as well, and it’s that tone’s success that makes Ufouria worth playing. The tweeness is overflowing from the screen. It invites comparison to the few times where Nintendo’s cutsier mascots found themselves in craftlike environments but the production here gives it a different feel. Look close enough at any of your characters and you can faintly see the individual strands of felt that construct their bodies and clothing. Whereas something like Yoshi’s Wooly World feels like it was made from fabrics that came together within its universe, Ufouria feels like it was made with fabrics that came together from our universe. Seemingly small distinction, but it gives the game a vibe a little closer to the best British cultural exports that put physical toys and models into fantastical environments for kids, like Thomas the Tank Engine and Brum. It’s a wonderful style whose only problem is that I wish it was pushed further: the random generation that the levels lean on limit Ufouria’s ability to produce meaningful setpieces and memorable singular objects in this style, as opposed to just tylesets and backdrops. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3169903247 That vibe is communicated beyond just the aesthetic, though. That old menu switching between characters is now a little high-five animation where they tag each other in. Everyone gets their own goofy walk cycle and their own chirpy little animal crossing voice. You’ll be hearing them a lot because friendly debriefs are a frequent occurrence. I’m largely willing to come to the defense of the fact that Ufouria’s actual gameplay can sometimes be intentionally simple, but there’s two areas where I found that the game's structure was inhibiting the tone and not helping it. The first is in Efouria’s ‘prepare for the final boss collection phase’, that has you going to new zones and completing them with whatever parameter that level defines (such as not getting damaged, doing it in under a time-limit, etc). It's the only notable difficulty spike within Ufouria and the spike isn’t the problem as much as the framework around it is: there’s no way to quick retry when you fail, demanding that you go home and trek all the way back to the zone to repeat its challenge. It’s annoying in a way the game otherwise never is. The second is that its random generation and collection focus fits horizontal levels far better than vertical: which is largely fine because vertical sections are the minority, but you can frequently miss a collectable you didn’t know was coming (its random, remember?) and lack an effective way to get back up to it—usually requiring a full retry. Hebe eventually learns to climb, but certain level layouts prohibit climbing due to ledges or other protruding objects. [h2] In Conclusion [/h2] Ufouria is a beautiful little game. Its lean on randomly generated worlds prevent the artstyle from producing memorable setpieces and occasionally cause some annoying pathfinding snags. It’s a game that’s at its best despite and not because of its gameplay, but it effectively recreates the tone of its 33 year old predecessor and infuses that recreation with its own style. Its blend of cartoonish characters with real fabrics and craft materials give the game a twee feel and it sustains that tweeness with its low stakes platforming and friendly themes. It’s only got a few hours of game, but that’s a slice of life worth giving. I had an amazing time playing Ufouria: The Saga 2. The world of Ufouria is truly unique and you can tell how much personality the game itself has. The characters are charming and their dialogues and interactions are super cute and funny. The UI is extremely polished and original, making menu navigation really enjoyable. The gameplay is really straightforward, you go exploring various platforming areas and collect coins you can use later in your HUB to buy upgrades in a vending machine. These upgrades can help you progress in new areas and even power up your characters. There is a boss fight at the end of each area too. I personally enjoyed the audio, it seemed fitting for the game atmosphere and the sound effects felt accurate. It took me around 5 hours to finish the main story while collecting various achievements. I still have some things to do in the game to obtain all achievements. The game felt extremely polished and I didn't find bugs during my playthrough. Most importantly: I had a LOT of fun playing this game. I totally recommend it to anyone who likes simple platformers and vivid game worlds. Looking forward to seeing more of the world of Ufouria and its characters in the future!

This game bills itself as a sequel to classic Metroidvania Ufouria, but it's not really that. It's not a game I'd describe as a sequel or a remake due to its very strange nature. If anything, Ufouria 2 is more of an incremental platformer. The desicion to completely move away from Metroidvania roots in favor of buying upgrades was likely chosen due to tight budget as it means the player will traverse levels over and over again. The levels themselves are somewhat random with pre-determined chunks building a new level each time. However, they're not that different each time. By all accounts, I feel like Ufouria 2 is a bit of a cheap trick. A weirdly grindy platformer that asks you to go through the samey levels, complete missions, collect coins and cans to purchase more things. However, it never feels bad. Each level is very short and the aesthetic is absolutely beautiful. There's also plenty of dialogue which reminds me a lot of Japanese 4-koma comics: silly, not exactly laugh-out-loud funny, but pretty witty and charming. It should also be mentioned that Ufouria 2 is a short game. If I wasn't going back to the beaten levels to collect stuff and see new things it's very likely I would've finished the game in 2 hours. I still recommend this game, but only if you understand what kind of game it is: it's not Ufouria again, nor is it a fully-fledged sequel, just a charming game about collecting stuff to buy more stuff. I liked it, but it might not be your cup of tea.

A long time ago a friend of mine had a NES so I went to his home every now and then, one of the games he had was something called "Ufouria" that I never heard of, but I was immediately hooked on it: it gave me an interest in metroidvanias (when they weren't called like that yet) and many years later brought me to write a series of articles about all the games in the series, that you can read [url=http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/hebereke-series-introduction/]starting from this one[/url]. So, when I heard that Sunsoft was bringing Ufouria back after like 3 decades, I was quite interested in what they were going to do with it so many gens later. The answer is: not that much. I found it not terrible but quite disappointing for what it is and its price. [b]Pros:[/b] - The new graphic style is really charming and a good innovation of the simple shapes and bright colors from the original 8-bit sprite-based graphics. Even rendering said pixels with perler beads is a cute choice and ties in with the "arts and crafts" new style. - Good arrangements of the already good soundtrack of the original game. - Good translation and adaptation that perfectly captures the goofy humour of the characters and their attitudes. [b]Cons:[/b] - Extremely easy, linear and railroaded. The plot is not that good that you can appreciate the game always pointing you on the right track instead of letting you explore more. - The "roguelite" structure makes it really repetitive. Procedural generation of the levels probably would not have worked, but the variations in levels are so minimal and you'll have to revisit them so many times in order to buy the required stuff from the machine, that you're going to get bored after a couple hours of always doing the same stuff. - The 4 new endgame areas are just rehashes of the previous ones. - Several buyable items are just cosmetic stuff that don't really change the gameplay in any way. When you have enough money and cans to buy the TV item that supposedly makes the game harder, not only the game is already close to the end, but there seems to be no difference in difficulty at all. - Characters' special moves are irrelevant (being buyable and, again, optional). The game is so easy that you will never need to use Hebe and Sukezaemon's special attacks, and by the time you get O-chan and Jennifer's special ability to reach cans in hard places, you've probably catched so many of these that you won't care to use them. Unless you're a completionist, but there's not even an achievement for that. - The achievement for gaining 50K coins at once is absurd and just a means to artificially increase the game's length, since it's way more than you need to buy all the stuff put together. - Not about the game itself, but it's not good that there's no option in the menu outside of changing the language, not even for the volume or screen resolution, or multiple save slots if you decide to start over. [b]Nitpicks:[/b] - The barrel cat/smiley face boss is missing. - The Donadona enemies (crawling guys on the giant tree) no longer spare Sukezaemon when he's crawling towards them. - Hebe clones/doppelgangers are present in other games, so it would make more sense to fight them in the boss rooms once you defeated your friends, instead of having to fight your friends' clones even if they are in your party already (mirror matches included). This is all... I would've preferred an 1:1 remake with new graphics or a totally new sequel instead of this strange and boring reboot/sequel hybrid.
Thank you Sunsoft for making one of the best sequels ever, can't wait for Hebereke 3: The wrath of Jennifer

yeah i dont know about this one. its carried entirely by its novelty. you play as some platforming mascot rejects who buy their character upgrades through a vending machine. everything is just at face value which is pretty funny. the music is great but its just remixes of the first game's music which just goes to show how great 8-bit music can be at setting the mood. but man the gameplay can get boring. the level design is NES tier random platforms and enemies everywhere. eventually it just turns into a coin grind. overall this game is worth it for its charm and it does try its best to carry the game. but it's definitely overpriced for what you get, i would say it's worth maybe $15.

This game will go down in history as one of the best reboots ever along with Blaster Master Zero, the world is a fully realised version of what the NES version attempted to do. The enemies now have names and lore, the characters frequently talk to each other and banter, the visuals are so gorgeous and the soundtrack is such a good listen, both the remixes and the brand new tracks! If you like Kirby, Goemon, Earthbound, Katamari and other cute and quirky Japanese games, you simply MUST experience this brilliant Saga. This game has infinite charm and soul. My heart would break if this game did poorly, it is everything you could ask for from a SunSoft comeback.

As a massive fan of the original game, this sequel honestly feels... confusing. It's like they really didn't know what to do with it [spoiler] which honestly makes sense considering this game was developed without the original Hebereke devs' knowledge [/spoiler] and it ultimately leads to a mess of an experience. For starters, none of the small details from the original game were carried over. The most glaring of these removals is the fact that Hebe no longer runs faster than the rest of the characters, giving you pretty much no reason to use him until you get the suction cups. Secondly, switching up the gameplay style from a metroidvania to more of a roguelite was definitely not the right move. There was so much potential to give Hebe and his pals a giant, sprawling world to romp around in, but instead they're confined to the same few short levels that are only negligibly different with each run-through. Hell, the four levels in which you find the rocket parts have absolutely NO reason to revisit them after you obtain the parts. No boss rematches, no Bobodori eggs, no challenge rooms, nothing. Finally, there are a myriad of aspects in this game that seem to be present for the sole purpose of padding it out. The original game is short as well, but at least there are parts that feel like somewhat of a challenge. Having to buy a particular item for each unlockable character in order to play as them is one of the most blatant examples of fluff in this game. And don't even get me started on the achievements. Having 50k coins at once? Seriously? All in all, this game definitely could have been pulled off much better. I feel like if the development of this game was at least overseen by the original devs, we could have had a much more coherent experience on our hands.

Art style, characters and sound effects are cutest thing ever. Would even say cutest out of all Hebereke games that I know off. Only thing lacking in Ufouria 2 is lack of post game content like true final boss, playable Ufouria 1 section (spoilers) [spoiler] which the ending showcased [/spoiler], and it does start to feel repetitive after you went through all the levels this game has to offer. [b] HUGE TIP [/b] Prioritise money collecting upgrades and avoid spending on optional upgrades because most of them are useless except hard mode. The reason for this is because there's an achievement that requires you to have huge amounts of money, which gets far worse if you buy all store items before you start hunting for it.
